citation_title: Beam-Driven Transverse Deflecting Structure for Femtosecond Electron-Beam Diagnostics
submission_history: Submission history From: Sergey Tomin [ view email ] [v1] Wed, 13 May 2026 16:33:08 UTC (1,919 KB) [v2] Fri, 15 May 2026 20:01:02 UTC (1,920 KB) [v3] Wed, 27 May 2026 14:10:31 UTC (1,920 KB)
abstract: Abstract: High-resolution longitudinal phase-space (LPS) diagnostics are essential for X-ray free-electron lasers and advanced accelerators. Conventional radio-frequency transverse deflecting structures (TDSs) provide direct femtosecond-scale LPS measurements, but their substantial RF-power and infrastructure requirements strongly limit their deployment at multi-GeV beam energies. Here, we propose a beam-driven transverse deflecting structure in which a leading driver bunch, separated by one RF bucket from a trailing witness bunch under study, excites long-lived wakefields in a resonant cavity array. By placing the witness bunch near a zero crossing of the wakefield, the bunch experiences an approximately linear time-dependent transverse kick. Electromagnetic simulations of the resonant structure, combined with start-to-end beam-dynamics simulations based on European XFEL parameters at a final beam energy of 14 GeV, demonstrate a temporal resolution of $\sim 1.6$ fs for a 500 pC driver bunch, with a clear scaling toward the sub-femtosecond regime at higher charge.

citation_title: Development of Sapphire-Based Solid-State Neutron Detectors for Fusion Environments
submission_history: Submission history From: Enrico Perelli Cippo Dr. [ view email ] [v1] Tue, 10 Nov 2026 21:10:15 UTC (1,176 KB)
abstract: Abstract: Single-crystal diamond is the reference solid-state technology for fast neutron detection in fusion devices. Despite this, its complex manufacturing increases their costs and puts limitations on their geometry. Moreover, the limits in their long-term stability and their behaviour in harsh environments further constraint its applications. Synthetic sapphire (Al2O2) is a promising alternative as a solid state detector material: it is available in large, low-cost wafers and features both a wider bandgap and a higher displacement energy compared to diamond. Despite this, it has so far received little-to-no attention as a neutron detector. This work presents the first steps of a development programme for sapphire-based fast neutron detectors. Eight prototypes with 4.5 x 4.5 mm2 and 9 x 9 mm2 active areas and 625 um thickness were fabricated from commercial wafers with Al-Si electrodes and coupled to different electronic configurations. All prototypes detected 5.47 MeV alpha particles from a 241Am source, confirming the viability of both the fabrication process and the use of sapphire as an active material. The small signals (30-40 mV over a peak-to-peak noise of about 8 mV) and the count rate increasing with bias indicate that sapphires will require higher electric fields than the ones experimented in the work (up to about 2.5 kV). Geant4 simulations were also used to estimate the response of a sapphire detector to 14.06 MeV (DT) neutrons, highlighting the perspectives of the detector as a fusion diagnostic.
